# Book III: Definitions

Euclid's words on the left, the Lean that stands for them on the right. Words with no Lean partner are never used in a Lean proof.


## Definitions

| | Euclid | Lean |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Equal circles are those the diameters of which are equal, or the radii of which are equal. | `EqualCircles`: a radius of the one is equal to a radius of the other |
| 2 | A straight line is said to touch a circle which, meeting the circle and being produced, does not cut the circle. | `Touches A B α`: the straight line AB meets the circle and does not cut it |
| 3 | Circles are said to touch one another which, meeting one another, do not cut one another. | `CirclesCut α β`: the circles meet at two points and each has a point within the other; `TouchesInternally α β C`: they meet at C, a point of β is within α, and no point of β falls outside α; `TouchesExternally α β C`: they meet at C, and no point is within both; `CirclesTouch α β C`: either touches the other within, or they touch without. Touching is read of the whole circles. Beside it is defined the reading at the point of contact, which Heath prefers. `TouchesInternallyAt α β C`: they meet at C, they are two circles, and near C no point of β falls outside α; `TouchesExternallyAt α β C`: they meet at C, and near C no point is within both; `CirclesTouchAt α β C`: either touches the other within, or they touch without, read at C. III.13's companions prove, for any two circles and any point, that each whole-circle definition holds exactly when its reading at the point does, so a statement may be read either way |
| 4 | In a circle straight lines are said to be equally distant from the centre when the perpendiculars drawn to them from the centre are equal. | `‖E F‖ = ‖E G‖`, for the perpendiculars EF, EG from the centre E (III.14); `Foot E A B F`: F is the foot of the perpendicular from E to AB, or E itself when AB passes through E, so that a diameter is at no distance (III.14 general) |
| 5 | And that straight line is said to be at a greater distance on which the greater perpendicular falls. | `‖E H‖ < ‖E K‖`, for the perpendiculars EH, EK from the centre E (III.15), or for the feet H, K, `Foot` (III.15 nearer) |
| 6 | A segment of a circle is the figure contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle. | `Arc`: a circle, the ends A, B of a straight line in it, and a point E naming its side, the segment AEB; its points, `InSegment`, and its circumference's, `OnArc`; segments that coincide, `Arc.Congruent` (III.24, III.26, III.28) |
| 7 | An angle of a segment is that contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle. | `MixedAngle.ofSegment A B α S`: the angle of the segment on S's side of AB, read as the region it opens near A; the companions of III.16 and III.31 compare it there with rectilineal angles placed along AB on that side |
| 8 | An angle in a segment is the angle which, when a point is taken on the circumference of the segment and straight lines are joined from it to the extremities of the straight line which is the base of the segment, is contained by the straight lines so joined. | `∠ A E B`, for a point E on the circumference of the segment |
| 9 | And, when the straight lines containing the angle cut off a circumference, the angle is said to stand upon that circumference. | `standing α B A C`, the circumference on which the angle BAC stands; the circumference BKC is `circumference α B K C`, and an arc's is `Arc.measure`; each measured as twice the angle that stands on it at the circumference |
| 10 | A sector of a circle is the figure which, when an angle is constructed at the centre of the circle, is contained by the straight lines containing the angle and the circumference cut off by them. | none: no proposition of Book III uses a sector |
| 11 | Similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, or in which the angles are equal to one another. | `∠ A E B = ∠ C F D`: equal angles in the segments AEB, CFD |
